- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes (e.g., 80+), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “rebound” or “mean reversion” effect.
- Model underestimates when true price drops below 70, particularly in the middle-to-late horizon (e.g., 65–60 range).
- Model shows persistent bias toward higher prices in the first 10–15 days, then drifts toward lower prices — suggests lag in adjusting to recent downward momentum.
- When history includes a recent spike (e.g., 80+), model often fails to reflect the “cooling-off” phase and overpredicts continuation.
- Model underestimates when true price is below 65, especially if recent history includes a sharp drop — suggests failure to recognize mean reversion or “bottoming” phase.
- Model tends to overcorrect after a sharp drop — e.g., if price drops to 60, model may forecast 70+ next period, missing the “recovery” or “rebound” phase.
- Model often fails to capture “tail risk” or “black swan” events — e.g., sudden drops below 60 after a spike — suggests lack of volatility adjustment.
- Model underestimates when true price is below 60, especially if recent history includes a sharp drop — suggests failure to recognize mean reversion or “bottoming” phase.
- Model tends to overestimate when true price is above 80, especially if recent history includes a spike — suggests failure to capture “cooling-off” or “rebound” phase.
